body_markdown:
My story begins when I was just a kid. My father owned some of what I thought were the most beautiful cars around.


I still remember the day, when I was 5 years old, that he came home with a brand-new 1960 Ford Thunderbird. It was black with a red interior, and it looked to me like a bullet on wheels. He traded in his cars in every three or four years, so after the ’60 T-Bird he had a ’63 and then a ’67. After that, though, he didn’t like the body style of the Thunderbird, so he came home with a 1970 Lincoln Continental coupe. And he had the same cadence with those, too: After the ’70 he had a ’73 coupe and finally[a ’77](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/lincoln/continental/1977/1977-lincoln-continental-base?id=aCn1I000000DWHgSAO) .


Donald Miller

Donald Miller


He kept the ’77 in great condition in the garage, and he would start it occasionally to keep the big 400-cubic-inch V-8 running in good order. He even put new tires on the car in later years, because they were looking unsafe, not because they were worn out.


My father had stopped driving the Lincoln but he didn’t want to sell it, so it sat in the garage for years. One day, I told him that I would buy it from him, because I didn’t want to lose the car to someone else. In 2015, when I turned 60, my father handed me a birthday card, and in it was the title for the Lincoln. I still drive it to this day, and it reminds me of the fun I had with my father and our cars.


Donald Miller
